findings.text: Approval can take six months, one year or longer in practice, well beyond the ED's prescribed timeline; applicants must follow up repeatedly with offices and officials to move applications forward.
The online system shows an application as 'returned' without displaying the specific objection, forcing applicants to contact offices to find out what correction is needed.
Prolonged approval affects project finances; one participant cites a ₹60,000 monthly liability resulting in a loss of more than ₹7 lakh over a year.
Applicants depend on architects and consultants to prepare plans, understand requirements and handle the approval process, adding professional expenditure.
Rainwater harvesting is treated as mandatory for approval; a participant suggests making it optional so applicants who skip it are not charged for it.
The defence/airport-clearance radius is seen as too wide; a participant suggests reducing it.
There is no single standard set of requirements followed consistently during inspections — different inspectors ask for different changes, creating confusion.
Participants propose a fixed processing time of 3, 5 or 7 days at each officer level, with the application automatically moving to the next level if the limit is exceeded.
In the renewal process, some documents already available from the earlier licence/application (including previously submitted certificates) remain in the system, reducing the need to resubmit.
Applications involving defence clearance take additional time; one case had the defence-related part alone take around 3-4 months.
Files remain pending at the Commanding Officer's office for around two months, extending the overall approval timeline.
Applicants face uncertainty about whether documents beyond those submitted online are required, with additional document requests arising mid-process.
The approval process includes physical site inspection and checks related to land-use zoning, plot area and permitted building floors.
Buildings in areas surrounding the airport are subject to additional NOC and height-permission requirements.
The online application process provides real-time tracking and is described as more convenient than the offline process.
The portal should show the exact objection on a returned application, and the same building requirements should be followed by all inspecting officers.
The online system should provide clear information on application status, applicable fees and other details so applicants do not have to depend on office visits.
Establish a clear timeline for completing the approval process, including departmental review and site verification.

gaps.text: The ED states the prescribed timeline is 60 days, with eligible low/medium-risk buildings (plot area up to 500 sq m) getting instant self-certified approval. FGD participants across both sessions instead report actual total approval times of 3-4 months (online) up to six months to over a year (offline/overall), with no participant describing receiving instant approval — the lived timeline businesses report is far beyond what the ED's 60-day figure (or the self-certification fast-track) would suggest.

The ED describes the fee basis as per-square-metre rates, land-area/land-use charges, a percentage of construction cost, and rainwater-harvesting charges, without quoting exact figures. FGD session 2 participants instead describe a flat recurring charge of 'every year 500' (₹500/year) plus unclear additional renewal-related costs — a different, specific figure that doesn't map cleanly onto the ED's stated fee basis, and FGD participants themselves say the exact fee structure is unclear.
FGD session 2 participants independently corroborate the ED's description of real-time online application tracking as a genuine, convenience-improving feature over the earlier offline process.

The user manual and examples do not clearly explain which requirements apply to each industry, making the application difficult to complete correctly.

The portal's user manual and the practical application process differ, making the manual hard to follow while completing the form.
Applicants cannot identify all required documents in advance and must check each application stage to find out which additional documents are needed.
Step-by-step disclosure of document requirements, plus differences between the manual and the actual process, cost applicants additional time identifying and collecting documents.
Delays occur while applicants wait for clarification from customer support on technical requirements and the correct ownership/entity category.
Provide a complete list of required documents at the start of the CTE process so applicants can prepare in advance.
Update the user manual with clear, practical examples showing which requirements and dropdown options apply to different industries.
Provide clear explanations of technical construction/water-pollution/air-pollution requirements, including documents needed for specific clearances.
Strengthen customer support to give timely clarification on technical queries and help with ownership/entity category selection.
Provide sector-wise details of applicable documents and requirements before applicants submit their applications.
Participants found the daily online clarification session (12:00 noon to 1:00 PM) helpful and recommend continuing it.
A water clearance certificate is shown as a portal requirement, but the specific document and issuing authority were unclear to participants.

findings.text: The electricity connection process lacks a clear, predictable timeline; applications take longer than expected with limited visibility into status or reasons for delay.
Online submission does not eliminate the need for physical follow-up — applicants may still need to visit the electricity office to check progress or get updates.
Non-availability of required infrastructure (cables, wires, meters) forces applicants to arrange these themselves, increasing overall cost.
Additional documents and requirements, particularly NOCs and property-related documents for commercial premises, can arise mid-process rather than being known upfront.
A shortage of line staff affects execution of connection-related work, contributing to delays.

A manufacturing unit's billing category was changed from industry to hotel/resort — raising its electricity rate — without the applicant being informed; the matter remained under grievance after a complaint was filed.
After online submission and payment, applicants lack clear online visibility of subsequent status, pending stage or expected timeline, making office visits necessary for updates.
Documents or NOCs are requested during processing, after the initial application, particularly for commercial properties.
Shortage of line staff affects execution of electricity-connection-related work.
Non-availability of required meters, cables or line infrastructure affects completion of the connection.
Electricity connections should be provided within a clearly specified period, such as 15, 40 or 45 days.
All required documents, NOCs and inspection-related requirements should be communicated upfront instead of being requested later.
Applicants should receive clear updates on processing status and pending stage instead of having to visit the office.
Electricity fluctuation affects equipment and is linked to maintenance, testing and certification requirements.
Distance between the premises and the transformer is raised as a factor in providing a connection.

The ED record does not address billing-category reclassification disputes (e.g. industry reclassified to hotel/resort, raising the tariff); FGD participants describe this happening without notice and remaining stuck in grievance — a real pain point outside what the ED documents.

When trained employees leave, new staff have to be retrained to manage fire-safety requirements.

Required corrections and safety measures should be identified clearly at the first inspection to avoid repeated modifications and inspections.
New rules and regulatory changes should reach concerned officers and applicants without delay, so applications aren't held pending implementation instructions.

Inspection should be carried out within a defined period after application so approval does not remain pending for long periods.

gaps.text: The ED states that Legal Metrology registration 'is granted on a one-time basis with lifetime validity (no renewal required, post-deregulation)', while separately noting that the weighing/measuring-instrument verification certificate is valid '1, 2 or 5 years depending on category'. Across two FGD sessions, participants instead describe 'the licence' itself as having a one-year validity with an annual ₹3,000 renewal fee (plus a late-renewal penalty), and a two-year/one-year split for mechanical vs electronic instruments (no 5-year category mentioned) — conflating what the ED frames as a lifetime, one-time registration with a recurring annual-renewal obligation, and citing validity bands that only partly match the ED's 1/2/5-year instrument-certificate figures.

FGD sessions give several different fee figures for Legal Metrology (₹200 for a 10 kg instrument, ₹400 for a 50 kg instrument, a ₹3,000 annual renewal fee, and a ₹500-per-quarter late-renewal charge) that are plausible within the ED's stated ₹10-₹5,000 range but are not cross-referenced against the ED's own fee schedule, so it is unclear whether these are the same fees the ED describes or additional charges.
All three FGD sessions report no redundant or duplicate document requirements for Legal Metrology, corroborating the ED's statement that redundant documents were removed following deregulation.

gaps.text: The RFNO ED states the Fire NOC 'is valid for five years' (with an annual undertaking submitted in the interim), but FGD participants describe 'the existing one-year validity period' and discuss extending it to five years — i.e. participants' lived understanding of the current validity (one year) directly contradicts the ED's stated five-year validity figure.
The ED's RFNO record does not mention the reported ~500 KB document-upload limit on the renewal portal, which FGD participants raise as a concrete submission difficulty.

One row of the FGD transcript's own quotes table pairs a 'Document Upload Limit' topic with a quote about 'establishments employing 20 or more workers' — content that belongs to the Shops & Establishment service, not Fire NOC renewal, suggesting a table-formatting/data-entry error in the source document; that row's content was not used as a Fire NOC finding or quote here.

gaps.text: The ED states registration validity 'is now valid for lifetime with no renewal required (amended from an earlier one-year validity)'. Across both FGD sessions, however, participants describe an active validity-expiry-and-renewal cycle: a notification is sent before 'the validity' expires, an additional one-month renewal window applies after expiry, and completing renewal in that window changes the registration number (creating the downstream problem of updating the new number across other documents/records). This describes a live renewal requirement that directly contradicts the ED's claim that renewal is no longer required.
Both FGD sessions independently confirm the ED's described shift to a fully online process (via NSWS) as a significant, positive improvement over the pre-2023 offline, paperwork-heavy process.

gaps.text: The ED describes GST tax filing as 'entirely online' through the GST portal, with physical visits 'not required for routine filing.' FGD participants, however, describe filing-related financial formalities — obtaining signatures on challans and ensuring documents meet bank-acceptance requirements — that sit outside the pure online-portal flow the ED describes, suggesting the process is not purely digital end-to-end for every business.
FGD participants corroborate the ED's description of entirely-online dashboard access for viewing filing details and monitoring submission status.

gaps.text: The ED's fee description states water-connection charges are a flat ₹50/month (one connection) or ₹60/month (two connections), with 'no separate application fee based on connection size... stated.' FGD participants instead describe commercial connection costs as a combination of 'registration fees, installation charges and labour costs' that vary 'according to the applicable category and work involved' — a more complex, variable fee structure than the flat monthly rate the ED described.

The ED gives no fixed timeline for water-connection processing ('no fixed departmental timeline... is specified'); FGD participants fill this gap with a specific lived figure — connections reportedly taking '20-30 days or longer' for commercial applicants — though this has not been confirmed against an official departmental target.
The ED leaves applicantOfficeVisit as 'unclear'; FGD participants resolve this ambiguity by confirming that visits to the department are in fact required for application-related formalities.
